opus-5.5.text:
I think science fiction is less a prophecy and more a kind of rehearsal. The best science-fiction writers aren't really predicting the future. They're taking something that already exists in the present, a technology, a social tension, a fear, and pushing it to its logical extreme so we can see it more clearly. So when people say "oh, this film predicted that," often it's because the author was simply a very sharp observer of their own time.

That said, I do believe science fiction shapes reality in a very real way, because it shapes the imagination of the people who build things. A lot of researchers in my field grew up reading Asimov, watching *2001*, *Blade Runner*, *Ghost in the Shell*. Those stories set up a mental picture of what an intelligent machine should look like, what it should be able to do, even what it should feel like to talk to one. So in a sense, it becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy. Not because the writer saw the future, but because engineers and scientists, consciously or not, try to build the thing they were dreaming about as kids.

For me personally, what's interesting is where science fiction got it wrong. For decades, the imagined AI was very symbolic, very logical, a cold robot reasoning step by step. What actually happened is much messier. It came from learning from huge amounts of data, it's statistical, it's sometimes surprisingly human-like in language but strangely weak in things a child finds easy, like understanding the physical world, spatial reasoning, common sense about objects. Very few stories anticipated that particular shape of intelligence.

And that's part of why I care so much about vision and world models. I think the sci-fi picture of an embodied intelligence, something that sees, moves, and understands the world, is still largely unrealized, even though we now have very fluent language models. So I treat science fiction as a source of inspiration and a set of questions, not a roadmap. It reminds us of what we might want, and what we should be afraid of. But the actual path, the real technical path, we still have to discover ourselves, and it usually looks nothing like the movies.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses sci-fi films and their influence, but does not say that films or television tend to portray bleak futures.

fable-5.1.text:
I think science fiction is less a prophecy than a mirror. The authors aren't predicting the future so much as taking a fear or a hope that already exists in the present and stretching it to its logical extreme. So when something in a novel "comes true," it's often because the seed was already planted in the time the author was writing. Asimov's robots, Clarke's satellites, Gibson's cyberspace — these weren't magic guesses. They were people paying very close attention to the technology around them and asking, "what happens if this keeps going?"

That said, I do think science fiction has a real effect on reality, just not in the direction people usually assume. It's not that the future obeys the fiction. It's that the fiction shapes the people who build the future. A lot of researchers I know, myself included to some degree, grew up on these stories. They give you a vocabulary and an image of what's possible before the technology exists. When we talk about "AI" in the lab, the mental picture many people carry around comes from films, not from the math. Sometimes that's inspiring, and sometimes it's a problem, because the fictional version is almost always more coherent and more dramatic than what we actually have.

For instance, in vision and multimodal research, people assume a model that can see and describe a scene must "understand" it the way a character in a film would. The reality is much messier. Our models are extremely good at some things and surprisingly fragile at others, and that uneven profile doesn't appear in science fiction, because it's not a good story. So I try to hold two things at once: I enjoy the stories, and I let them push my imagination, but I'm careful not to let them define what success looks like. The most interesting outcomes in my career have been the things no novel anticipated — scaling laws, the strange emergent behaviors, the way data quality matters more than clever architecture. The future tends to arrive sideways, not head-on.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses science fiction as a mirror and its influence on researchers, but does not say that science-fiction films or television tend to portray bleak futures.

astra-6.text:
I think science fiction is more useful as a way to imagine possibilities than as a literal prediction of the future. A novel or a film can start with a question—what if machines could think, or what if intelligence became abundant—and explore what that might mean for people. It doesn’t have to explain every technical step to make that question valuable.

There’s also a feedback loop. People grow up seeing these imagined futures, and some of them become researchers or engineers who try to build something similar. So when reality starts to resemble science fiction, it may be partly because the fiction helped shape what people wanted to create.

But I’d be careful about treating a compelling story as evidence that a particular future is inevitable. The interesting question for me is less, “Did this film predict the technology?” and more, “What assumptions did it make about how we would live with it?”

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses science fiction as a way to imagine possibilities and shape future technology, but does not say that films or television works tend to portray bleak futures.

sol-6.1.text:
I tend to see science fiction less as prophecy and more as a way of exploring possibilities. A novelist can start with an idea—say, that machines become intelligent—and ask what that would mean for how we live, how we relate to each other, or how society is organized. They don’t have to explain every engineering step along the way.

As researchers, we have to work through those steps. Something can feel inevitable in a film and still turn out to be extraordinarily difficult in practice. And the reverse happens too: a technology arrives in a form that nobody really imagined, because the constraints and incentives shape it differently.

But fiction can also influence the future. Someone sees a film when they’re young, becomes fascinated by an idea, and spends their career trying to build it. So when reality resembles science fiction, it isn’t necessarily that the author predicted the future. Sometimes the story helped inspire it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses science fiction as a way to explore possibilities and inspire technology, but does not say that films and television tend to portray bleak futures.
